passage: On Sunday evening in Dublin, Freya opened a video call and held her list up to the camera. Her brother Gabriel was in his kitchen in Cork, and Aunt Maeve, their mother's sister, had a mug in her hands. "Mum needs about twelve hours of help a week," Freya said. "Hospital visits, bills, phone check-ins, sorting her tablets into the weekly box. I can't do all of it with my job." Gabriel spoke first. "I'll take the finances and drive her to the hospital." "And I'll do the daily calls and set up the tablet box," said Freya. Aunt Maeve added, "I'll go round on Saturdays for tea." They wrote it down and sent it round. Nobody said it was perfect, but everybody knew what was theirs.

qa.q: Which jobs did Gabriel say he would take?
qa.a: Gabriel said he would take the finances and drive their mother to the hospital.

qa.q: What was Freya feeling when she said "I can't do all of it with my job"?
qa.a: Freya felt stretched and worried about coping alone, though she was ready to ask for help clearly.

qa.q: What could the family do if Aunt Maeve's Saturdays become hard to keep?
qa.a: They could look at the list again after a month and move tasks around or add paid help, since it is a shared plan.

qa.q: How might Gabriel have felt being asked directly?
qa.a: Gabriel may have felt glad to have clear tasks he could do, rather than a vague worry about his mother.

grounding: Freya calls her brother and aunt, states the tasks and time needed, and each takes a share.

passage:
The family room at the Kochi hospital was small, with one window and a box of tissues. Chaitanya, the hospital's social worker, had offered it for the meeting.
Anupama had asked her brother Dhruv and their aunt, Leela aunty, to come. Their mother was being discharged on Friday.
"I've written down what Amma will need," Anupama said, and read it out. "Doctor visits twice a month. Medicines sorted every week. Bills and insurance papers. Someone to call her every day."
"That's a lot," Dhruv said.
"It is. I can't do it all and keep my job. So I'm asking each of us to take a part."
Dhruv took the finances and hospital visits: "I'm good with paperwork, and my office is near here." Leela aunty took daily calls and organising the weekly pill box. Anupama kept the weekends and the doctor's reports.
Chaitanya wrote it all on a care sheet and gave each of them a copy.

qa.q: When was their mother being discharged?
How did Anupama seem to feel asking her family to share the work?
qa.a: She seemed determined and honest, though probably anxious, admitting she couldn't do it all and keep her job.

qa.q: What else could the family do to keep the arrangement working?
qa.a: They could meet or call once a month to check how the split is going and adjust if their mother's needs change.

qa.q: How might Dhruv see his part in the plan?
qa.a: Dhruv sees a clear, suitable role that fits his skills and office location, which likely makes him more willing and confident to help.

grounding: It shows a daughter calling her brother and aunt, stating the tasks and time needed, and asking each to take a part, with him handling finances and hospital visits.

passage:
Subject: Papa's care — let's share it

Dear Francis and Lucy aunty,

Thank you both for picking up on Sunday. I've been thinking since then about how to divide Papa's care fairly, because I can't keep doing it all alone alongside my new job.

Here's what he needs each month, as far as I can tell:
- Two hospital visits for his heart check-ups, about half a day each.
- Paying bills, insurance claims and pension paperwork, a few hours.
- A phone call every day to check how he's feeling.
- Sorting his medicines into the weekly box every Sunday.

My suggestion: Francis, you take finances and hospital visits, since you have the car and know the bank. Lucy aunty, would you do the daily calls and the medicine box? He listens to you. I'll take weekends at home and keep in touch with his doctor.

Can we speak on Saturday to confirm?

Love,
Sunaina

qa.q: How many hospital visits does Papa need each month?
qa.a: Two hospital visits for his heart check-ups.

qa.q: How does Sunaina seem to feel in the email?
qa.a: Sunaina seems tired and stretched from doing it all alone, but hopeful that sharing the work fairly will help.

qa.q: What else could Sunaina do if Francis or Lucy aunty can't take on their part?
qa.a: Sunaina could ask what part they could manage, or look into paid help for the missing tasks.

qa.q: How might Lucy aunty feel about being asked to call daily?
qa.a: Lucy aunty may feel valued, since Sunaina notes that Papa listens to her, and the task is clear.

grounding: It shows a daughter writing to her brother and aunt with the tasks and time needed, asking him to take finances and hospital visits and the aunt daily calls and medicines.
